pos: adj. (fallen into ruin; the state of a fortified city God has thrown down)
etymology: Latin ruinosus, from ruere, to fall. In the KJV the word attaches almost always to heaps — the rubble a defenced city becomes when its defences are answered.
biblical_def: The LORD tells Sennacherib that his conquests were assignments: “Hast thou not heard long ago how I have done it, and of ancient times that I have formed it? now have I brought it to pass, that thou shouldest be to lay waste fenced cities into ruinous heaps” (2Ki 19:25), and Isaiah records the same words (Isa 37:26). Damascus receives the sentence directly: “Behold, Damascus is taken away from being a city, and it shall be a ruinous heap” (Isa 17:1). Isaiah states the principle in praise: “thou hast made of a city an heap; of a defenced city a ruin… it shall never be built” (Isa 25:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ruinous as fallen to ruin; entirely decayed; demolished; and also destructive, pernicious, bringing or tending to bring ruin.
webster_full: RUINOUS, a. Fallen to ruin; entirely decayed; demolished; dilapidated; as an edifice, wall or fence that is ruinous.
RUINOUS, a. Destructive; pernicious; bringing or tending to bring ruin; as a ruinous project.
RUIN, n. Destruction; fall; overthrow; defeat; that change of any thing which destroys it.
scriptures: Hast thou not heard long ago how I have done it, and of ancient times that I have formed it? now have I brought it to pass, that thou shouldest be to lay waste fenced cities into ruinous heaps.
Isa 17:1
The burden of Damascus. Behold, Damascus is taken away from being a city, and it shall be a ruinous heap.
Hast thou not heard long ago, how I have done it; and of ancient times, that I have formed it? now have I brought it to pass, that thou shouldest be to lay waste defenced cities into ruinous heaps.
Isa 25:2
For thou hast made of a city an heap; of a defenced city a ruin: a palace of strangers to be no city; it shall never be built.
corruption_summary: Assyria's conquests were God's work assigned long before Assyria existed, and the empire that boasted of them was the axe rather than the arm.
corruption_paragraphs: Second Kings 19:25 is one of the most sweeping statements of divine sovereignty in Scripture, and it is addressed to a pagan emperor at the height of his pride. I have done it; of ancient times I have formed it; now have I brought it to pass, that thou shouldest be to lay waste fenced cities into ruinous heaps. Sennacherib's campaigns were an ancient decree executed on schedule. Isaiah 10 supplies the moral accounting: Assyria is the rod of God's anger, sent against a hypocritical nation — howbeit he meaneth not so, neither doth his heart think so. God ordained the act; Assyria supplied the malice; and God punished the malice He had ordained the act through, which is exactly the pattern of Acts 2:23 at the cross.

The corruption to name is the false dilemma that says either God governs and man is not culpable, or man is culpable and God does not govern. Scripture holds both without embarrassment and never resolves the tension by surrendering either half. Joseph's brothers meant it for evil, God meant it for good; Assyria is the axe and is broken for boasting against the hand that swings it; Herod and Pilate did whatsoever God's hand and counsel determined before to be done. The comfort in it for the church is enormous: no empire is improvising, and no ruinous heap is an accident.
roots_summary: Hebrew gal nitstsim, ruinous heaps; mappalah (H4654), a ruin, heap of rubbish; batsar (H1219), to fortify, make defenced.
roots_lines: Hebrew mappalah (H4654) — ruin, heap of rubbish; Isaiah 17:1, 23:13, 25:2.
Hebrew gal (H1530) — heap, wave; 2 Kings 19:25, Isaiah 37:26.
Hebrew batsar (H1219) — to fortify, cut off, make inaccessible; 2 Kings 19:25, Jeremiah 33:3.
Hebrew yatsar (H3335) — to form, fashion, purpose beforehand; Isaiah 37:26, 43:1.
Hebrew massa (H4853) — burden, oracle of judgment; Isaiah 17:1, 13:1.
usage: “Of ancient times that I have formed it” — the campaigns Assyria thought were its own.
“Damascus is taken away from being a city” — and shall be a ruinous heap.
“Of a defenced city a ruin” — Isaiah's song over the fall of the proud.

pos: v. (reduced to poverty; made destitute, whether by an oppressor or by a judgment)
etymology: Old French empovrir, from Latin in- + pauper, poor. In the KJV the word covers both the poverty inflicted by enemies and the poverty of a man too poor to bring an offering.
biblical_def: Under Midian the nation was stripped: “Israel was greatly impoverished because of the Midianites; and the children of Israel cried unto the LORD” (Jdg 6:6) — a judgment that began, as Judges always begins, with sin: “the children of Israel did evil in the sight of the LORD: and the LORD delivered them into the hand of Midian seven years” (Jdg 6:1), until they “made them the dens which are in the mountains, and caves, and strong holds” (Jdg 6:2). Isaiah shows a poverty that does not stop a man from idolatry: “He that is so impoverished that he hath no oblation chooseth a tree that will not rot; he seeketh unto him a cunning workman to prepare a graven image, that shall not be moved” (Isa 40:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to impoverish as to make poor, to reduce to indigence, and also to exhaust strength or richness, as of land.
webster_full: IMPOVERISH, v.t. To make poor; to reduce to poverty or indigence; as, idleness and vice impoverish a man.
IMPOVERISH, v.t. To exhaust strength, richness or fertility; as, to impoverish land by frequent cropping.
INDIGENCE, n. Want of estate, or means of comfortable subsistence; penury; poverty.
scriptures: Jdg 6:1
And the children of Israel did evil in the sight of the LORD: and the LORD delivered them into the hand of Midian seven years.
Jdg 6:2
And the hand of Midian prevailed against Israel: and because of the Midianites the children of Israel made them the dens which are in the mountains, and caves, and strong holds.
Jdg 6:6
And Israel was greatly impoverished because of the Midianites; and the children of Israel cried unto the LORD.
He that is so impoverished that he hath no oblation chooseth a tree that will not rot; he seeketh unto him a cunning workman to prepare a graven image, that shall not be moved.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 40 shows a man with nothing left for an offering scraping together the price of an idol, which is the exact measure of what sin does to judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 40:19-20 is quiet satire and deadly serious. The rich man overlays his god with gold and casts silver chains; the poor man, so impoverished that he has no oblation, still finds a tree that will not rot and hires a cunning workman — and his one concern is that the finished god shall not be moved. He cannot afford to worship the LORD and he can afford this. Idolatry is not a luxury of the prosperous; it is the native industry of the fallen heart at every income, and the last thing a man gives up.

The corruption to name is the modern account that treats religious devotion as a function of circumstances — poverty explaining superstition, prosperity explaining secularity, so that idolatry becomes a symptom rather than a sin. Romans 1 puts it the other way round: men knew God, glorified Him not as God, became vain in their imaginations, and changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image. The cause is not deprivation but suppression of truth. Judges 6 shows the sequence exactly: they did evil, they were impoverished, and only then did they cry unto the LORD.
roots_summary: Hebrew dalal (H1809), to be brought low, made thin; cakan (H5533), to be impoverished; terumah (H8641), oblation, heave offering.
roots_lines: Hebrew dalal (H1809) — to be brought low, made poor; Judges 6:6, Psalm 79:8.
Hebrew cakan (H5533) — to be poor, impoverished; Isaiah 40:20 only.
Hebrew terumah (H8641) — oblation, offering lifted up; Isaiah 40:20, Exodus 25:2.
Hebrew pesel (H6459) — graven image; Isaiah 40:19, 40:20, Exodus 20:4.
Hebrew zaaq (H2199) — to cry out; Judges 6:6, Exodus 2:23.
usage: “Israel was greatly impoverished because of the Midianites” — and then they cried.
“So impoverished that he hath no oblation” — and still he buys an idol.
“A graven image, that shall not be moved” — the poor man's only requirement.

pos: v. (burnt on the surface; of seed without root, and of men under the fourth vial)
etymology: Middle English scorchen, probably from Old French escorcher, to flay. The Greek of the parable is kaumatizo, to be burned by heat — the same verb John uses of the men under the vial.
biblical_def: In the parable of the sower the sun is the test: “when the sun was up, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered away” (Mat 13:6), and Mark records it the same (Mar 4:6). The seed had sprung up fast — “forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth” (Mat 13:5) — and Christ names the sun: “when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended” (Mat 13:21). Revelation uses the same word for the fourth vial: “men were scorched with great heat, and blasphemed the name of God… and they repented not to give him glory” (Rev 16:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to scorch as to burn superficially; to subject to a degree of heat that changes the color of a thing, or both color and texture of the surface.
webster_full: SCORCH, v.t. To burn superficially; to subject to a degree of heat that changes the color of a thing, or both the color and texture of the surface.
SCORCH, v.i. To be dried up; to be parched with heat.
WITHER, v.i. To fade; to lose its native freshness; to become sapless.
scriptures: Mat 13:5
Some fell upon stony places, where they had not much earth: and forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth:
Mat 13:6
And when the sun was up, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered away.
Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended.
Rev 16:9
And men were scorched with great heat, and blasphemed the name of God, which hath power over these plagues: and they repented not to give him glory.
corruption_summary: The stony-ground hearer sprang up fastest and lasted least, and Christ names persecution as the sun that exposes him.
corruption_paragraphs: The second soil is the most dangerous, because it looks like the best. It springs up forthwith; it receives the word with joy; it outpaces the good ground in the early weeks. And it has no root, so the first heat finishes it. Christ's diagnosis is precise: he dureth for a while, and when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended. The trouble is not general hardship but cost incurred for Christ specifically. The sun does not make the plant rootless; it reveals that it always was.

The corruption to name is any evangelism that engineers the stony ground on purpose — that measures success by speed and volume of response, presses for immediate visible decision, and treats initial joy as conversion. The parable exists because Christ knew the phenomenon and expected His church to meet it. The Reformed insistence that regeneration is a work of God producing root, and that perseverance is the evidence rather than the optional extra, is not coldness toward converts; it is the pastoral application of Matthew 13. Revelation 16 shows the same hardness at the end: scorched, and blaspheming, and repenting not.
roots_summary: Greek kaumatizo (G2739), to scorch, burn with heat; rhiza (G4491), root; skandalizo (G4624), to be offended, made to stumble.
roots_lines: Greek kaumatizo (G2739) — to scorch; Matthew 13:6, Mark 4:6, Revelation 16:8, 16:9.
Greek rhiza (G4491) — root; Matthew 13:6, 13:21, Romans 11:16.
Greek skandalizo (G4624) — to offend, cause to stumble; Matthew 13:21, 11:6.
Greek xeraino (G3583) — to dry up, wither; Matthew 13:6, Mark 11:20.
Greek thlipsis (G2347) — tribulation, pressure; Matthew 13:21, John 16:33.
usage: “When the sun was up, they were scorched” — the fastest growth, the shortest life.
“Because they had no root, they withered away” — the sun revealed, it did not cause.
“Men were scorched with great heat, and blasphemed” — judgment without repentance.

pos: v. (withered by a scorching wind; of grain struck barren before harvest)
etymology: Old English blaest, a blowing or blast. The agricultural sense is the east wind off the desert, which the Hebrew names shadaph — to scorch, to blight.
biblical_def: Pharaoh's second dream: “behold, seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind sprung up after them” (Gen 41:6), which he retold as “seven ears, withered, thin, and blasted with the east wind” (Gen 41:23), and Joseph interpreted — “the seven empty ears blasted with the east wind shall be seven years of famine” (Gen 41:27). Isaiah uses the same picture of nations Assyria had swept: their inhabitants “were as the grass of the field, and as the green herb, as the grass on the housetops, and as corn blasted before it be grown up” (Isa 37:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to blast as to make to wither by some pernicious influence, as too much heat or a noxious wind; and blasted as blighted, ruined.
webster_full: BLAST, v.t. To make to wither by some pernicious influence, as too much heat or moisture, or other destructive cause; as, to blast corn.
BLAST, n. A sudden gust or gale of wind; also, a pernicious or destructive influence upon animals or plants.
BLIGHT, n. Anything nipping or blasting; that which destroys the health of plants.
scriptures: Gen 41:6
And, behold, seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind sprung up after them.
And, behold, seven ears, withered, thin, and blasted with the east wind, sprung up after them:
And the seven thin and ill favoured kine that came up after them are seven years; and the seven empty ears blasted with the east wind shall be seven years of famine.

Therefore their inhabitants were of small power, they were dismayed and confounded: they were as the grass of the field, and as the green herb, as the grass on the housetops, and as corn blasted before it be grown up.
corruption_summary: Amos lists blasting among the mercies God sends, because a judgment intended to bring a nation back is not cruelty.
corruption_paragraphs: Amos 4:9 belongs in any account of this word: I have smitten you with blasting and mildew… yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD. The blasting east wind is listed with famine, drought, pestilence and overthrow in a series of five, each ending with the same refrain. God is reciting a sequence of disciplines that failed, and He recites them as evidence of patience rather than of wrath — each one was an opportunity, and each was declined. The chapter ends with the summons: prepare to meet thy God, O Israel. Blasting is the lesser judgment sent to prevent the greater.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's temporal judgments on nations are mercies in intent, aimed at repentance. Two errors surround this and both are common. The first is the confident identification of particular calamities with particular sins, which Christ forbade in Luke 13 concerning the tower in Siloam. The second is the refusal to read any national trouble as the hand of God at all, which Amos 4 makes impossible for anyone who takes the prophets seriously. The right response is not a diagnosis of one's neighbours but the summons Amos gives: prepare to meet thy God.
roots_summary: Hebrew shadaph (H7710), to scorch, blast; shiddaphon (H7711), blasting, blight; qadim (H6921), the east wind.
roots_lines: Hebrew shadaph (H7710) — to scorch, blast; Genesis 41:6, 41:23, 2 Kings 19:26.
Hebrew shiddaphon (H7711) — blasting, blight; Amos 4:9, Deuteronomy 28:22, 1 Kings 8:37.
Hebrew qadim (H6921) — east wind; Genesis 41:6, Exodus 10:13, Hosea 13:15.
Hebrew shibbol (H7641) — ear of grain; Genesis 41:5, Judges 12:6.
Hebrew raab (H7458) — famine; Genesis 41:27, Amos 8:11.
usage: “Seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind” — Pharaoh's second dream.
“Seven years of famine” — Joseph's reading of the blasted ears.
“As corn blasted before it be grown up” — nations swept by Assyria.

pos: v. (to ring or thrill with a sharp sensation; used only of ears hearing a report of judgment)
etymology: Middle English tinglen, a variant of tinkle, of imitative origin. The Hebrew tsalal means to ring or quiver — the sound left in the ears after a blow.
biblical_def: Three times in the Old Testament God announces a judgment so severe that the report of it will ring in the ears of those who hear. To Samuel, of the house of Eli: “Behold, I will do a thing in Israel, at which both the ears of every one that heareth it shall tingle” (1Sa 3:11). Of Manasseh's Jerusalem: “Behold, I am bringing such evil upon Jerusalem and Judah, that whosoever heareth of it, both his ears shall tingle” (2Ki 21:12). And through Jeremiah at the valley of the son of Hinnom: “I will bring evil upon this place, the which whosoever heareth, his ears shall tingle” (Jer 19:3) — the reason given plainly: “because they have hardened their necks, that they might not hear my words” (Jer 19:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to tingle as to feel a kind of thrilling sound, and to feel a sharp thrilling sensation, as the ears do at hearing a very loud sound.
webster_full: TINGLE, v.i. To feel a kind of thrilling sound; as, the ears tingle.
TINGLE, v.i. To feel a sharp thrilling pain; as, the teeth tingle.
THRILL, v.i. To feel a sharp piercing sensation running through the body.
scriptures: And the LORD said to Samuel, Behold, I will do a thing in Israel, at which both the ears of every one that heareth it shall tingle.
Therefore thus saith the LORD God of Israel, Behold, I am bringing such evil upon Jerusalem and Judah, that whosoever heareth of it, both his ears shall tingle.
Jer 19:3

And say, Hear ye the word of the LORD, O kings of Judah, and inhabitants of Jerusalem; Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Behold, I will bring evil upon this place, the which whosoever heareth, his ears shall tingle.

Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Behold, I will bring upon this city and upon all her towns all the evil that I have pronounced against it, because they have hardened their necks, that they might not hear my words.
corruption_summary: The first tingling word came against a priest who knew his sons' wickedness and restrained them not.
corruption_paragraphs: First Samuel 3 is a judgment on a good-natured man. Eli was not himself a scandal; he was devout, he trained Samuel, he received the sentence with submission — it is the LORD: let him do what seemeth him good. And the charge against him is exact: because his sons made themselves vile, and he restrained them not. The failure was not appetite but authority declined. A father and a priest who would not use the office God gave him, and the house was cut off for ever. It is the first of the three tingling judgments, and it falls inside the sanctuary rather than on the nations.

The corruption to name is the redefinition of fatherly and pastoral gentleness as the refusal to restrain. Eli did speak to his sons — 1 Samuel 2:23 records the conversation, and it is a reasonable, wounded, ineffective appeal. What he would not do was remove them. Scripture treats the tolerance of known wickedness in those under one's charge as complicity, whether in a household or in a church, and 1 Timothy 3 makes a man's rule of his own house the test of his fitness to take care of the church of God. Gentleness that will not act is not the fruit of the Spirit; it is the abdication Eli was judged for.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsalal (H6750), to tingle, quiver, ring; ozen (H241), ear; qashah oreph, to harden the neck.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsalal (H6750) — to tingle, quiver; 1 Samuel 3:11, 2 Kings 21:12, Jeremiah 19:3.
Hebrew ozen (H241) — ear; 1 Samuel 3:11, Psalm 40:6, Isaiah 50:5.
Hebrew qashah (H7185) — to be hard, harden; Jeremiah 19:15, Exodus 7:3.
Hebrew oreph (H6203) — neck, back of the neck; Jeremiah 19:15, Deuteronomy 31:27.
Hebrew kahah (H3543) — to be dim, to restrain feebly; 1 Samuel 3:13.
usage: “Both the ears of every one that heareth it shall tingle” — against the house of Eli.
“Whosoever heareth of it, both his ears shall tingle” — against Manasseh's Jerusalem.
“Because they have hardened their necks” — the reason given every time.

pos: v. (to shake, tremble; of the earth at God's presence and of men at the sight of Him)
etymology: Old English cwacian, to tremble. Hebrew ragaz, to be agitated or moved; the Greek of Matthew 27 is seio, the root of seismos — the word for an earthquake.
biblical_def: Creation quakes at its Maker. Joel: “The earth shall quake before them; the heavens shall tremble: the sun and the moon shall be dark” (Joe 2:10). Nahum: “The mountains quake at him, and the hills melt, and the earth is burned at his presence” (Nah 1:5). At the death of Christ the same thing happens at the same moment as the veil: “the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent” (Mat 27:51). And Hebrews recalls Sinai, where the mediator himself trembled: “so terrible was the sight, that Moses said, I exceedingly fear and quake” (Heb 12:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to quake as to shake; to tremble; to be agitated with fear or cold; and notes it is used of the earth as well as of persons.
webster_full: QUAKE, v.i. To shake; to tremble; to be agitated with quick but not violent motions; as, the earth quakes.
QUAKE, v.i. To tremble; to shudder; to be agitated with fear or cold.
TREMBLE, v.i. To shake involuntarily, as with fear, cold, or weakness.
scriptures: Joe 2:10
The earth shall quake before them; the heavens shall tremble: the sun and the moon shall be dark, and the stars shall withdraw their shining:
Nah 1:5
The mountains quake at him, and the hills melt, and the earth is burned at his presence, yea, the world, and all that dwell therein.
And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent;
And so terrible was the sight, that Moses said, I exceedingly fear and quake:)
corruption_summary: Hebrews sets quaking Sinai against Mount Zion to show what the gospel changed and what it did not.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 12 contrasts two mountains. At Sinai there was the mount that might be touched and that burned with fire, blackness, darkness and tempest, a voice the hearers begged to stop, and a mediator who said I exceedingly fear and quake. Believers are not come to that mount; they are come to Mount Zion, the city of the living God, to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling. But the chapter does not end in relief. It ends: see that ye refuse not him that speaketh — for our God is a consuming fire. The terror is removed by the blood, not by a change in God.

The corruption to name is the widespread assumption that the New Testament replaced a fearful God with an approachable one, so that reverence is a leftover of the older covenant. Hebrews 12:28-29 forbids it in a single sentence: let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear, for our God is a consuming fire. The earth quaked at Golgotha, not at Sinai only, and it quaked because the Son of God was dying. The Christian's liberty of access is bought and real, and it is access to the God the mountains quake before.
roots_summary: Hebrew ragaz (H7264), to quake, be agitated; raash (H7493), to shake, quake; Greek seio (G4579), to shake, cause a quaking.
roots_lines: Hebrew ragaz (H7264) — to quake, tremble, be agitated; Joel 2:10, Psalm 4:4.
Hebrew raash (H7493) — to shake, quake; Nahum 1:5, Isaiah 13:13.
Greek seio (G4579) — to shake, quake; Matthew 27:51, Hebrews 12:26.
Greek entromos (G1790) — trembling, terrified; Hebrews 12:21, Acts 7:32.
Greek ekphobos (G1630) — exceedingly afraid; Hebrews 12:21, Mark 9:6.
usage: “The mountains quake at him, and the hills melt” — Nahum on the presence of God.
“The earth did quake, and the rocks rent” — at the death of Christ.
“I exceedingly fear and quake” — Moses at Sinai.

pos: v. (to tread underfoot; of victory over the enemy, of contempt shown to holy things, and of the winepress of wrath)
etymology: Middle English trampelen, frequentative of trampen, to tread. Hebrew ramas, to tread down; the Greek katapateo of Matthew 7 is to trample down under the feet.
biblical_def: The word runs in three directions. Victory: “Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder: the young lion and the dragon shalt thou trample under feet” (Psa 91:13), promised to the man of whom God says, “Because he hath set his love upon me, therefore will I deliver him” (Psa 91:14). Contempt: “Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you” (Mat 7:6). And wrath: “I have trodden the winepress alone… for I will tread them in mine anger, and trample them in my fury” (Isa 63:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to trample as to tread under foot, especially with pride, contempt or insult; to tread down; to prostrate by treading.
webster_full: TRAMPLE, v.t. To tread under foot; especially, to tread upon with pride, contempt, triumph or scorn.
TRAMPLE, v.t. To tread down; to prostrate by treading; as, to trample grass or grain.
TRAMPLE, v.i. To tread with force and rapidity.
scriptures: Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder: the young lion and the dragon shalt thou trample under feet.
Because he hath set his love upon me, therefore will I deliver him: I will set him on high, because he hath known my name.
Mat 7:6
Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.
Isa 63:3

I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me: for I will tread them in mine anger, and trample them in my fury; and their blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments, and I will stain all my raiment.
corruption_summary: Christ commands discrimination in the handling of holy things, which is not the opposite of evangelism but part of it.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 7:6 sits immediately after judge not and is placed there on purpose. Christ forbids hypocritical condemnation in verse 1 and requires discerning judgment in verse 6 — a man must be able to tell a dog from a sheep and a swine from a lamb to obey it at all. The command is about the treatment of holy things: there are hearers who will not merely reject the truth but trample it and turn again and rend the one who brought it, and the Lord does not require His servants to keep pressing it on them. Paul shakes his raiment at Corinth and turns to the Gentiles; the disciples are sent out with instructions about shaking off dust.

The corruption to name is the flattening of judge not into a prohibition on all discernment, which is the single most quoted and least understood sentence in the New Testament. The same Sermon on the Mount requires the hearer to recognize false prophets by their fruits, to distinguish two gates and two ways, and to withhold pearls from swine. Judging in the sense forbidden is condemning others by a standard one exempts oneself from — the beam and the mote. Judging in the sense commanded is the exercise of a sanctified mind on what is true and who is trustworthy, and 1 Corinthians 2:15 says the spiritual man judgeth all things.
roots_summary: Hebrew ramas (H7429), to trample, tread down; darak (H1869), to tread, as a winepress; Greek katapateo (G2662), to trample underfoot.
roots_lines: Hebrew ramas (H7429) — to trample, tread down; Psalm 91:13, Isaiah 63:3, Daniel 8:7.
Hebrew darak (H1869) — to tread, bend a bow, tread the winepress; Isaiah 63:3, Psalm 91:13.
Greek katapateo (G2662) — to trample underfoot; Matthew 7:6, 5:13, Hebrews 10:29.
Greek margarites (G3135) — pearl; Matthew 7:6, 13:46, Revelation 21:21.
Hebrew purah (H6333) — winepress; Isaiah 63:3, Haggai 2:16.
usage: “The young lion and the dragon shalt thou trample under feet” — the promise of Psalm 91.
“Lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you” — the pearls.
“I will tread them in mine anger, and trample them in my fury” — the winepress.

pos: n. (a shuddering dread; in Genesis the darkness that fell on Abram before the covenant was cut)
etymology: Latin horror, a bristling, a shuddering, from horrere, to bristle with fear. Hebrew eymah, terror; pallatsuth, shuddering; zilaphah, the burning horror of indignation.
biblical_def: Before God made the covenant with Abram, He put him out of the way: “when the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell upon Abram; and, lo, an horror of great darkness fell upon him” (Gen 15:12). David knows it in flight: “Fearfulness and trembling are come upon me, and horror hath overwhelmed me” (Psa 55:5). Psalm 119 gives it a righteous object: “Horror hath taken hold upon me because of the wicked that forsake thy law” (Psa 119:53). Ezekiel gives it to a people under judgment: “horror shall cover them; and shame shall be upon all faces” (Eze 7:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines horror as a shaking, shivering or shuddering, as in the cold fit which precedes a fever; and a powerful excitement of fear and dread, or terror mingled with detestation.
webster_full: HORROR, n. A shaking, shivering or shuddering, as in the cold fit which precedes a fever.
HORROR, n. An excessive degree of fear, or a painful emotion which makes a person tremble; terror; a shuddering with fear.
HORROR, n. Terror or dread mingled with detestation; that which excites horror.
scriptures: And when the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell upon Abram; and, lo, an horror of great darkness fell upon him.
Psa 55:5
Fearfulness and trembling are come upon me, and horror hath overwhelmed me.
Horror hath taken hold upon me because of the wicked that forsake thy law.
Eze 7:18
They shall also gird themselves with sackcloth, and horror shall cover them; and shame shall be upon all faces, and baldness upon all their heads.
corruption_summary: Abram was put to sleep in horror and darkness while God alone passed between the pieces, which is why the covenant cannot fail.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 15 is the foundation of the doctrine of the unconditional covenant. The animals are divided and the pieces laid opposite each other in the ordinary form of a covenant-cutting, in which both parties walk the aisle and invoke on themselves the fate of the beasts if they break faith. Abram never walks it. A horror of great darkness falls on him, he sleeps, and a smoking furnace and a burning lamp pass between the pieces alone. God binds Himself on both sides. Every promise in that covenant therefore rests on the faithfulness of one party, which is why Hebrews 6 calls it two immutable things in which it is impossible for God to lie.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that horror is not always a symptom to be relieved. Psalm 119:53 attaches it to a righteous cause — horror hath taken hold upon me because of the wicked that forsake thy law — and the psalmist offers it as evidence of love for God, not as a disorder. Scripture has room for a settled dread at what sin is and where it goes. The therapeutic instinct that treats every strong negative feeling as pathology cannot make sense of that verse, and a church that has lost the capacity for it will not be able to make sense of Ezekiel 7 either.
roots_summary: Hebrew eymah (H367), terror, dread; pallatsuth (H6427), shuddering, horror; zilaphah (H2152), burning indignation.
roots_lines: Hebrew eymah (H367) — terror, dread; Genesis 15:12, Exodus 15:16, Job 9:34.
Hebrew pallatsuth (H6427) — shuddering, horror; Psalm 55:5, Isaiah 21:4, Ezekiel 7:18.
Hebrew zilaphah (H2152) — burning horror, indignation; Psalm 11:6, 119:53.
Hebrew tardemah (H8639) — deep sleep; Genesis 15:12, 2:21, 1 Samuel 26:12.
Hebrew berith (H1285) — covenant; Genesis 15:18, 17:7.
usage: “An horror of great darkness fell upon him” — Abram while God passed alone.
“Horror hath overwhelmed me” — David in flight.
“Horror hath taken hold upon me because of the wicked” — horror with a righteous cause.

pos: n. (darkness, dimness; in Isaiah the condition God promises to reverse)
etymology: Latin obscuritas, darkness, from obscurus, covered over, dim. Isaiah uses the Hebrew ophel and chosek — the gloom that hides both the way and the walker.
biblical_def: Obscurity in Isaiah is always a condition God intends to end. Of the day of the Messiah: “in that day shall the deaf hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity, and out of darkness” (Isa 29:18). Of the fast God chooses: “if thou draw out thy soul to the hungry, and satisfy the afflicted soul; then shall thy light rise in obscurity, and thy darkness be as the noonday” (Isa 58:10). And of a nation that has forfeited it: “we wait for light, but behold obscurity; for brightness, but we walk in darkness” (Isa 59:9). Isaiah 60:2 sets the promise against the dark: “the darkness shall cover the earth… but the LORD shall arise upon thee.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines obscurity as darkness, want of light; a state of retirement from the world or from public notice; and a state of being unknown or unnoticed.
webster_full: OBSCURITY, n. Darkness; want of light.
OBSCURITY, n. A state of retirement from the world; a state of being unknown; privacy; as, to live in obscurity.
OBSCURE, a. Dark; destitute of light; not clear; also, not easily understood.
scriptures: And in that day shall the deaf hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity, and out of darkness.
And if thou draw out thy soul to the hungry, and satisfy the afflicted soul; then shall thy light rise in obscurity, and thy darkness be as the noonday:
Isa 59:9
Therefore is judgment far from us, neither doth justice overtake us: we wait for light, but behold obscurity; for brightness, but we walk in darkness.
Isa 60:2
For, behold, the darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the people: but the LORD shall arise upon thee, and his glory shall be seen upon thee.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 58 ties the lifting of a man's personal darkness to his treatment of the hungry, and says so in a chapter about fasting.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 58 begins with a complaint from a religious people: wherefore have we fasted, and thou seest not? God answers by describing the fast He chose — to loose the bands of wickedness, to deal thy bread to the hungry, to bring the poor that are cast out to thy house — and then attaches promises to it: thy light shall break forth as the morning, thy light shall rise in obscurity, and thy darkness be as the noonday. The chapter is not teaching that mercy earns God's favour. It is teaching that a devotion which leaves a man's neighbour hungry is a devotion God does not recognize, and that the darkness such a man complains of is his own.

The corruption to name has two forms and Isaiah 58 refutes them together. The first is the religion of forms without mercy, which the chapter is written against directly. The second is the modern reading that takes Isaiah 58 as proof that social action is the gospel and quietly drops the sabbath-keeping, the turning away of the foot, and the calling of the LORD's day a delight that the same chapter demands with equal force. The prophet joins what both parties separate. The light that rises in obscurity is promised to a people who fast rightly, keep the sabbath gladly, and feed the poor from the same heart.
roots_summary: Hebrew ophel (H652), gloom, thick darkness; chosek (H2822), darkness; tsohorayim (H6672), noonday.
roots_lines: Hebrew ophel (H652) — darkness, gloom, obscurity; Isaiah 29:18, 58:10, Job 3:6.
Hebrew chosek (H2822) — darkness; Isaiah 59:9, 60:2, Genesis 1:2.
Hebrew tsohorayim (H6672) — noon, noonday; Isaiah 58:10, Genesis 43:16.
Hebrew zarach (H2224) — to rise, shine forth; Isaiah 58:10, 60:2, Malachi 4:2.
Hebrew araphel (H6205) — gross darkness, thick cloud; Isaiah 60:2, Exodus 20:21.
usage: “The eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity” — the day of Messiah.
“Then shall thy light rise in obscurity” — promised to the fast God chose.
“We wait for light, but behold obscurity” — a nation's confession.

pos: n. (a cure; that which repairs an evil — and in Scripture, most often, the thing that is finally absent)
etymology: Latin remedium, from re- + mederi, to heal. In the KJV the word appears chiefly in the phrase without remedy, describing the point past which mercy has been refused too long.
biblical_def: Chronicles gives the epitaph of the kingdom: God “sent to them by his messengers, rising up betimes, and sending; because he had compassion on his people, and on his dwelling place” (2Ch 36:15), “But they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and misused his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD arose against his people, till there was no remedy” (2Ch 36:16). Proverbs states the same law twice: “shall his calamity come suddenly; suddenly shall he be broken without remedy” (Pro 6:15), and “He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy” (Pro 29:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a remedy as that which cures a disease; and that which counteracts an evil of any kind, repairs a loss, or restores a right.
webster_full: REMEDY, n. That which cures a disease; any medicine or application which puts an end to disease and restores health.
REMEDY, n. That which counteracts an evil of any kind; cure; that which repairs loss or disaster.
REMEDY, v.t. To cure; to heal; to repair; to remove or counteract an evil.
scriptures: And the LORD God of their fathers sent to them by his messengers, rising up betimes, and sending; because he had compassion on his people, and on his dwelling place:
But they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and misused his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD arose against his people, till there was no remedy.
Pro 6:15
Therefore shall his calamity come suddenly; suddenly shall he be broken without remedy.
Pro 29:1
He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy.
corruption_summary: Second Chronicles 36 sets the longest patience in Scripture beside the phrase till there was no remedy, and both belong to the same God.
corruption_paragraphs: The last chapter of Chronicles is one long sentence about patience running out. God sent by His messengers, rising up betimes and sending — the Hebrew idiom is of a man rising early, day after day, because he had compassion on His people and on His dwelling place. That is the reason given for the sending: compassion. And the response was mockery, contempt, and abuse of the prophets, until the wrath of the LORD arose till there was no remedy. Nebuchadnezzar burned the house of God, and the chronicler records that the land kept her sabbaths. The exile was not God losing His temper. It was the end of a long and specific mercy that had been refused.

The corruption to name is the presumption that there is always more time. Proverbs 29:1 addresses it directly, and its terms are exact: the man is often reproved, he hardeneth his neck, and the destruction is sudden and without remedy. Not one of those clauses describes an accident. Universalism in its confident forms and practical delay in its ordinary form make the same wager, that the door does not close. Scripture says it closes, and gives the illustration of a generation that had prophets rising up betimes and could not be bothered. Today, if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts.
roots_summary: Hebrew marpe (H4832), healing, cure, remedy; shakam (H7925), to rise early, do a thing betimes; qashah oreph, to harden the neck.
roots_lines: Hebrew marpe (H4832) — healing, remedy, cure; 2 Chronicles 36:16, Proverbs 6:15, 29:1, Jeremiah 8:15.
Hebrew shakam (H7925) — to rise early, do betimes; 2 Chronicles 36:15, Jeremiah 25:4.
Hebrew laab (H3931) — to mock, deride; 2 Chronicles 36:16 only.
Hebrew qashah (H7185) — to harden; Proverbs 29:1, Exodus 13:15.
Hebrew shabar (H7665) — to break, shatter; Proverbs 6:15, Jeremiah 19:11.
usage: “Rising up betimes, and sending; because he had compassion” — the reason for the prophets.
“Till there was no remedy” — the epitaph of Judah.
“Often reproved hardeneth his neck… and that without remedy” — the law stated twice.
